title_original: ‘Gondhal’ Director Santosh Davakhar Talks Creating India’s 2027 Oscar Entry, the Films That Inspired Him and More

blocks.text: India’s official selection for the 2027 Academy Awards is “Gondhal,” the debut feature film from director Santosh Davakhar. Following a screening of the film, Davakhar sat down with Variety ‘s Jazz Tangcay to discuss creating his debut, the Oscar movies that inspired him and the Indian heritage he wants to share through the film.

The film is set in 1960, a post-colonial era where illiteracy was prevalent and women were not afforded agency, Davakhar said. He purposefully chose to that setting and designed the Suman character based on how her situation would have been.

blocks.text: “You will feel that she is clever, she is manipulative, she’s selfish, but she’s just a 17-year-old girl,” Davakhar said. “She’s very young girl and she’s not allowed to break the barriers imposed by society. So she’s not openly challenging to the patriarchy, but she’s slowly making her choices.”

The title of the film is “Gondhal,” named for the traditional night-long devotional ritual performed for a newly married couple, and the film’s plot unfolds during the ritual. The main instrument used during the ritual is on the brink of disappearing because electrical ones are taking its place.

“We recorded it live as they performed because if we record this music at studio and then we ask them to perform, the energy will be different,” Davakhar said. “I want that real energy. I want that real devotion. That was a choice to document these instruments and so that the next generation can see, they can feel it and they can keep it alive.”

Much of the film takes place at night, which created unique challenges. Davakhar said they had over one kilometer of lighting. It took seven days to complete the opening shot, which has two or three stitches, and 22 days for the entire project. The music for the film was composed by Ilaiyaraaja. Davakhar said the 83-year-old Indian composer agreed to work on the film on the condition that he visited the remote village the film shot at to watch the ritual.

“He traveled over there 1,700 kilometers,” Davakhar said. “He watched this ritual which lasted until the morning. And then he went back to the studio and then he composed the music for this film. He’s a really great thing. And that’s why we Indians call him a god of music.”

The film opens with a 25-minute oner, and Davakhar said he was inspired by watching the 2001 Oscar-nominated, Hindi-language film “Lagaan.” It lost the Best Foreign Language Film award to “No Man’s Land,” and Davakhar wanted to understand why.

“When I watched it, I got to know that the powerful cinema is not only about the great actor or a great production budget or a great production value,” he said of watching “No Man’s Land.” “It’s also important about the powerful story, the powerful screenplay and the powerful craft.”

Davakhar was not allowed to watch film in theaters because his family considered that a luxury. He recalled watching 40 films in 15 days when his short “Adnyat” screened at Cannes. After that, he closely watched Oscar-winning films and noted “Birdman,” “1917” and “Roma” as movies that particularly fascinated him.

“That’s how I understood that the one take is important as storytelling because it allows you to flow with the story,” he said. “It doesn’t have any visual disruption. That’s why I wrote a film which could be in one take.”

From his experience at Cannes, Davakhar learned that the global perception of Indian cinema was limited. He wanted to change the perception that Indian cinema is around poverty or classism, so he focused on portraying Indian heritage proudly.
“That heritage will be the backdrop of the story, but the human emotion, human conflict, that will be the story,” he said.
